title: Chapter 6 Test: Portfolio Readiness
description: Ten questions on presenting the work — repository hygiene, résumé bullets, honest self-assessment and keeping the knowledge alive.

questions.prompt: Which résumé bullet is strongest for a support engineering role?
options: Passionate about cloud technologies and eager to learn
Responsible for database performance monitoring
Reduced a reporting query from a clustered index scan to a seek by removing a non-SARGable predicate, cutting logical reads from 12,400 to 38
Extensive experience with SQL Server, Python, AWS, Azure, Docker and Kubernetes
questions.explanation: It names a specific technique, a specific diagnosis and a measured outcome — and it hands the interviewer an obvious follow-up you can answer well. The others state enthusiasm, responsibility rather than action, or an unsubstantiated list.

questions.prompt: You discover a credential was committed to a public repository four minutes ago. What is the first action?
options: Delete the file in a new commit
Rotate the credential immediately, then clean the history
Make the repository private
Add the file to .gitignore
questions.explanation: Deleting the file in a later commit does not remove it from history, and making the repo private does not un-leak it. Automated scanners find keys pushed to public GitHub within seconds — assume it is compromised and rotate first.

questions.prompt: Which formatting choices help a CV survive an Applicant Tracking System? Select all that apply.
options: Single-column layout with standard headings
PDF with selectable text
Skill-rating bars and icons to show proficiency
The same terminology the job description uses, for skills you genuinely have
questions.explanation: ATS parsers mangle columns, tables, text boxes and graphics. Rating bars convey nothing machine-readable and are frequently dropped entirely. Keyword alignment is legitimate; keyword stuffing for things you cannot discuss is not.

questions.prompt: You should list every technology you have ever touched, to maximise keyword matches.
questions.explanation: An interviewer will pick something from the list at random. 'I used it in a personal project' is fine; 'I don't really know it' undermines everything else on the page. If you touched it once for twenty minutes, leave it off or put it under a clearly marked 'Familiar with' line.

questions.prompt: What should the first screen of a portfolio README contain?
options: The full installation instructions
What the project does, plus an architecture diagram
A list of every dependency and its version
Your contact details and a photo
questions.explanation: Assume ninety seconds of attention. Most readers form their opinion from the diagram before reading a word. Installation belongs further down; dependency lists belong in a manifest file.

questions.prompt: Your deployed demo costs money to keep running. What is the best option for the README?
options: Leave the dead link — reviewers will understand
Remove all mention of deployment
Note that it is torn down to control cost, link the infrastructure code, and give a docker compose command to run it locally
Replace it with a screenshot only
questions.explanation: A dead link is worse than no link. Explaining the teardown reads as cost discipline rather than abandonment, and a one-command local run gives the reader a way to try it anyway.

questions.prompt: Why is a 'can do with documentation' section in a capability inventory valuable?
options: It pads out a thin CV
Calibrated confidence is a signal in itself — knowing the edges of your knowledge makes you easier to trust on call
It is required by most ATS systems
It replaces the need for a skills section
questions.explanation: Saying 'I can read a Kubernetes manifest and I know what the components do, but I would not claim to run a cluster' is far stronger than a vague claim that collapses under one follow-up question.

questions.prompt: Match each maintenance activity to a sensible cadence.

pairs.left: A small addition to a project
Check cloud bills and the live deployment

questions.explanation: The fortnightly project addition is the one that compounds — a repository with commits spread over months reads completely differently from one with a six-week burst and then silence.

questions.prompt: You are getting no interview responses. Which is the **least** likely cause at this stage?
options: The CV is not surviving ATS parsing
You have applied to too few roles
Your technical knowledge is insufficient
Your LinkedIn headline does not contain the terms recruiters search for
questions.explanation: After six weeks of building deployed, documented projects, the constraint is almost never technical. Formatting, volume, discoverability and repository legibility are all more likely — and all faster to fix.

questions.prompt: What is the test you should run on your README with someone who has never seen the project — named by its duration?
questions.explanation: Give it to two people for ninety seconds, then ask what it does, what it uses, why one decision was made, and whether they would want to talk to the author. If they cannot answer the first two, the summary and diagram are buried.
